title: The Garden in Bloom
reflection: Which flower have I noticed in my child this week, and how could I name it quietly and give it room to grow?

questions.q: According to Lesson 13, where do the qualities that bloom in a child, such as patience, come from?
o: They are skills a parent installs through steady practice and reward over the years.
They are the one infinite power of the Self, showing through as will, knowledge and action.
They are inherited from whichever parent shows them most plainly at home.
They are gifts that some children have in plenty, while others have little within.
questions.e: At the centre of every child is the Ātman, the infinite repository of every excellence. Its one power flows out as will (icchā), then knowledge (jñāna), then action (kriyā). The power is the same in all; only its expression differs, like bulbs of different wattage on one current. The flowers are not planted by the parent.
questions.c: Every excellence flows from one infinite power

questions.q: A twelve-year-old’s report says “bright but distracted”, yet he spent four patient hours helping his grandmother with a new phone. Which response fits Lesson 13?
o: Treat the report as unfair, and tell him teachers cannot see what he is worth.
Wait to see whether the patience appears again at school before saying anything.
Notice the patience, name it quietly, and give it room, without ignoring the homework.
Begin with the homework, and mention the patience as a reward once marks improve.
questions.e: A parent looks to strengths rather than shortcomings, and does not begin with the problems. Many children arrive with flowers already in bloom. An observant parent watches for them, recognises them and encourages them to grow still further, and the weeds are not pretended away.
questions.c: Begin with what is beautiful and already there

questions.q: A mother told her eldest, again and again, that he was hopeless with money. Why does he still say it of himself decades later?
o: He has simply failed with money over the years, and so the words proved to be true.
A child looks to the parent to learn who he is, and words heard daily become his own thought.
He holds a grudge against his mother, and repeats her words so as to remember it.
Children forget what is said to them, and adults repeat it to excuse their own choices.
questions.e: The parent’s mind is the mirror in which a child is trying to see himself, and what the mirror shows, he comes to believe. A thought heard again and again lays down saṁskāras, and the mind begins to flow that way. The reflection a parent offers becomes the child’s own thought about himself.
questions.c: The parent is the mirror the child believes

questions.q: A parent of a ten-year-old whose marks have slipped wants to encourage her, not flatter her. Which words fit Lesson 13?
o: “You can do better. There is more in you than this result shows.”
“You are perfect as you are, and nothing needs to change.”
“Everyone else in the class did badly too, so do not worry.”
“Try harder next time, or you will be left behind.”
questions.e: Flattery soothes, but encouragement calls a young person higher. It urges them toward a greater manifestation and is not afraid to challenge: you can do better, there is infinite power within you. Words of encouragement empower a child to trust herself.
questions.c: Encouragement calls higher; flattery only soothes

questions.q: “A comfortable, easy and pleasant upbringing is the surest way to wake a child’s sleeping soul.”
questions.e: A soul is not roused by comfort. Fire appears from wood only through sustained friction, and muscles grow only through exercise. Swami Vivekananda calls the world a grand moral gymnasium. A wise parent does not clear every obstacle away, but provides the setting for honest hard work, and the struggle through which the soul awakes.
questions.c: The soul wakes through effort, not comfort

questions.q: A sixteen-year-old has drifted for two years and seems asleep inside. Which step fits Lesson 13?
o: Make his days easy and pleasant, and wait patiently for him to wake of himself.
Remind him each week of how much he is wasting his chances in life.
Entrust him with a real responsibility suited to his strength, and then trust him.
Hand him an ideal to read about, and ask for a written account of what it taught.
questions.e: A real responsibility, entrusted according to a young person’s capacity, can wake what comfort never will, as when a coach asks a teenager to train the juniors. Other settings are a challenge suited to strength, a chance to serve, beauty, and good company. Teenagers wake through ideals and through being trusted.
questions.c: Real responsibility and trust wake the sleeping soul

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a parent should invite growth and never hurry it?
o: A child who is pushed will always rebel in the end, so pushing never works at all.
The young should be given their own time, and the parent should step well away.
Growth that comes late is always stronger than growth that comes early in life.
Each one grows at their own pace, as a banana ripens sweeter on the tree.
questions.e: Effort, yet never haste. Each one grows at their own pace, and everything comes in its own season. A parent may long for the best in the shortest time, but it is wiser not to override the law of natural growth, and lose what would come so beautifully in its own time. The invitation is always there; the pressure is not.
questions.c: Invite and tend; never hurry the season

questions.q: A sixteen-year-old has seemed low and withdrawn for several weeks, and shows no interest in anything. Which response fits Lesson 13?
o: Offer more challenges at once, since the soul wakes through friction and effort.
Keep encouraging, and also speak to a doctor or a counsellor, as this needs care.
Wait for the winter to pass, since each one grows in their own season and time.
Praise a different strength each day, and the low mood will lift in good time.
questions.e: Dr Watson’s plain word: if a young person seems not just asleep inside but low or withdrawn for weeks, please speak to a doctor or a counsellor. That needs care as well as patience. Swamiji’s reply was “both together”: the patient tending of the garden, and the right help beside it.
questions.c: Low for weeks means care as well as patience

questions.q: “A good deed is best done where others can see it, since being seen is what makes kindness grow.”
questions.e: Kindness is not for the world to see; it is for one’s own growth, a flower that blooms whether or not anyone walks by. In an age of social media a parent watches and gently guides, so that goodness never turns into a performance. The quiet word, where only the two can hear, is the more powerful.
questions.c: Kindness blooms quietly, not as a performance

questions.q: A family wants a home that celebrates kindness as gladly as it celebrates marks. Which habit fits Lesson 13?
o: Each person names one good thing seen that day, at the table or at bedtime.
Each child earns a small reward for every kind act that the parents happen to see.
The parents keep a chart of every child’s good deeds, to be read out on Sundays.
The family posts its kind acts online, so that others may be inspired by them.
questions.e: Such a home keeps simple habits of noticing the good and saying so, at the table, at bedtime, or quietly in a corner. What a young person discovers in this way is worth more than praise from others. A child comes to know from within, “I am someone who helps,” and later, that the same light is in everyone.
questions.c: A home awake notices the good and says so
